Federated learning allows several manufacturers to train a shared surrogate without exchanging data. We study which federated optimizer brings such a surrogate closest to one trained on pooled data. On DrivAerNet++, we train a Transolver surrogate across six clients that each hold cars of a single body type, and we compare three spectral optimizers, which orthogonalize the update of each weight matrix (FedMuon and two methods we propose, FedMARS-M and FedOLion), with three non-spectral ones (FedAvg, SCAFFOLD-Adam and FedLion), all tuned with the same protocol. FedMuon and FedMARS-M reach a drag error within 2% of centralized training with Muon, using two to four local epochs per round. The non-spectral methods perform best with sixteen local epochs, the largest number we tested, and still have a 17 to 37% higher drag error than FedMARS-M. We relate this gap to the low stable rank of the weight gradients, for which an orthogonalized step yields about twice the first-order decrease of a gradient step of the same spectral norm. Code: https://github.com/armanbolatov/fedmarsdrivaernet

papers.title: ScaleDiag: Diagnosing the Limits of Test-Time Scaling in GUI Grounding
papers.authors: Chen Liu, Zhen Fang, Xin Yu, Dadong Wang et al.
papers.summary: GUI grounding maps a screenshot and a natural language instruction to the coordinates of the intended interface element. Existing approaches improve grounding through visual scaling, instruction scaling, and sampling scaling, yet it remains unclear which grounding bottlenecks these strategies address and where their gains saturate. To address this gap, we introduce ScaleDiag, a controlled diagnostic framework that isolates the effects of visual input, instruction information, and prediction sampling on GUI grounding by independently varying target scale and surrounding context, target-specific information and auxiliary descriptions, and candidate coverage and selection, respectively. We evaluate ScaleDiag across five benchmarks and up to eight vision-language models and find that each scaling strategy operates within a much narrower regime than commonly assumed. (1) Visual scaling is governed by target occupancy rather than a fixed crop ratio, with full-screen errors typically rescued once the target occupies only 0.32% of the cropped view, while further zooming eventually becomes harmful. (2) Instruction scaling is driven by information that identifies the target rather than description richness itself, as even ground-truth-derived attributes such as color, size, and shape are often neutral or harmful, while appearance and spatial descriptions account for over 90% of the achievable gain. (3) Repeated sampling exposes a different limitation, as correct coordinates are frequently generated but remain difficult to select, leaving 5.1–11.0 points of oracle headroom while geometric consensus provides almost no improvement. Together, these results show that test-time scaling is constrained by distinct operating regimes rather than benefiting monotonically from more visual focus, richer instructions, or additional samples. Our code is available at https://github.com/YenanLiu/ScaleDiag.

papers.title: CalibCache: Cache-to-Full Feature Dynamics Calibration for Diffusion Transformers
papers.authors: Mingyu Liang, Dingkun Xu, Jingwei Xu
papers.summary: Diffusion Transformers generate high-quality images, but iterative sampling remains computationally expensive. Feature caching reduces the number of full network evaluations, yet its approximation error can become more severe under short sampling schedules, where fewer full-compute steps and a coarser sampling grid can make history-based extrapolation less reliable. In this paper, we propose CalibCache, a lightweight offline calibration method that corrects systematic discrepancies between cached and full-compute feature dynamics. Specifically, CalibCache calibrates feature acceleration, defined as the second-order finite difference across sampling steps. Using only a single pair of full-compute and naive-cache trajectories at each setting, CalibCache fits scalar acceleration maps offline by centered least squares. These maps are then applied during sampling without additional full-network evaluations or online optimization. Across FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image on DrawBench and DiT-XL/2 on ImageNet-256, CalibCache consistently improves fidelity or generation quality over TaylorSeer under 20-step sampling at cache intervals N=3,4,5. At N=5, it reduces FLUX.1-dev LPIPS from 0.563 to 0.429 while achieving a 2.86× denoising speedup over full-compute sampling, and lowers DiT-XL/2 FID from 16.39 to 10.37 relative to TaylorSeer.

papers.title: Modeling Learner-Technology Interaction Through Multilevel Gaze Transition Dynamics to Inform Usability in Online Learning
papers.authors: Yueqi Weng, Jie "Jennifer" Lu, fan Yang
papers.summary: Gaze data provide fine-grained evidence of how learners engage with instructional content and interface elements, complementing conventional usability evaluation methods. However, eye-tracking analyses often examine within-slide visual attention and across-slide navigation separately, limiting understanding of learner interaction throughout extended learning experiences. This exploratory multi-method study integrated area-of-interest transitions, gaze entropy, slide-level navigation, and network-based representations to analyze seven eye-tracking recordings of high school students interacting with an AI-supported online biology lesson, complemented by three post-intervention focus groups. Results showed individual differences in within-slide gaze allocation and switching patterns. Learners followed shared navigation pathways but differed in revisiting and immediate return behaviors. The focus group findings highlighted positive perceptions of interactive materials and AI-generated feedback, alongside usability concerns related to navigation, interface clarity, and assessment guidance. Together, these outcomes show how integrating multilevel gaze analytics with learner perspectives can provide complementary evidence for identifying interaction trends relevant to usability evaluation. Future research should test this approach with larger, more diverse samples and examine relationships among gaze patterns, usability, and learning outcomes.

papers.title: Cross-Question Reliable Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Hector G. Rodriguez, Marcus Rohrbach
papers.summary: AI systems operating near the limits of their capabilities can maximize utility while minimizing the risk of error by abstaining or deferring questions they are not confident about to a human or a stronger model. Recently, large language models (LLMs) have been post-trained to estimate confidence in their own answers. To achieve this, methods reinforce confidence scores based on the correctness signal to each question-answer pair individually, with rewards that encourage assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect answers. However, estimating confidence scores is useful in that it enables selecting only the most confident answers, to maximize the share of solved questions while accommodating the user's risk tolerance. Assigning confidence 1 to correct answers and 0 to incorrect ones is theoretically optimal, but unattainable in practice and detrimental for selective prediction with a non-zero risk tolerance: confidences pushed to 0 and 1 carry no information about how answers compare to one another. We therefore introduce CARE (Cross-question Abstention Reward Estimation), which computes rewards over a set of question-answer pairs: At each of several risk tolerances, the confidences across the set induce an abstention threshold, and each confidence is rewarded for lying on the correct side of it. Since the threshold itself comes from the set, every verbalized confidence is reinforced relative to other questions' confidence, not against its own binary correctness label. On math, CARE increases the coverage at 5% risk (C@5) across MATH-500, GSM8K, and Big-Math-Digits from 0.8% to 42.4%, compared to existing pointwise correctness-matching rewards. When trained on multi-hop Wikipedia QA from HotpotQA, CARE improves C@5 in out-of-distribution general-knowledge, reasoning, and math benchmarks (including CommonsenseQA, GPQA, SimpleQA, and TriviaQA) from 12.3% to 23.6%.

papers.title: LLMs Are Already Confidence-Aware Zero-Shot Classifiers
papers.authors: Owen Cook, Xingyi Song
papers.summary: Zero-shot large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as text classifiers, but their labels are only useful when we know to what extent we can trust them. We compare black-box methods (verbalised confidence and sampling) with white-box methods that read token probabilities (P(True), and multiple logit-scoring methods using constrained generation). We evaluate eleven open-weight LLMs (1B-32B parameters) on five classification datasets with 3 to 151 labels, measuring classification performance (accuracy, F1-macro), discrimination (AUROC), and calibration (ECE and Brier score). The choice of confidence method rarely impacts accuracy significantly, but logit-based scoring methods lead to much better discrimination (AUROC 0.74-0.77) than black-box methods (AUROC 0.57-0.66). Replacing labels with single-token identifiers preserves discrimination but costs 3-6 accuracy points on average. We also introduce decision-only scoring, which only scores positions where labels diverge in the prefix tree (trie). It reduces decode steps by 88-96% on the three largest label sets and performs comparably to full-label scoring. The best open-weight model-method configurations (Gemma 4 31B and Qwen 3.5 9B) are competitive with the commercial Jev 1.13.0 classifier.

papers.title: TRACE-5G: Trust-Aware Runtime Attestation and Continuous Enforcement for 5G User Equipment
papers.authors: Al Nahian Bin Emran, Rajendra Paudyal, Rajendra Upadhyay, Arupjyoti Bhuyan et al.
papers.summary: The standard 5G Authentication and Key Agreement protocol (5G-AKA) authenticates subscriber credentials but does not verify the integrity of user equipment (UE). Existing literature includes admission-time device-certificate authentication and Trusted Platform Module (TPM)-based measured-boot attestation, which can additionally verify that the UE presents enrolled device credentials and boots into an approved state. However, these checks do not reveal whether harmful unauthorized software is executed after admission. We present TRACE-5G, which continuously verifies the UE's runtime software state and uses the resulting trust state to control network access. TRACE-5G retains the pre-admission certificate and boot checks, and in addition places the admitted UE in restricted connectivity while runtime integrity is verified. Linux Integrity Measurement Architecture (IMA) records runtime software measurements, TPM PCR (Platform Configuration Register) cryptographically accumulates them, and Keylime, a remote-attestation framework, repeatedly evaluates TPM and IMA evidence against enrolled references. A Trusted result grants full access on the existing PDU session, but an Untrusted result withholds or removes full access and causes network deregistration. We implement TRACE-5G on an srsRAN/Open5GS testbed with a hardware TPM2.0 UE and core-side firewall enforcement. Across ten trusted trials, Level 2 access was established in 9–12s. Across ten untrusted trials, promotion was consistently withheld; in a representative trace, restrictive policy was applied within 5ms of the Untrusted decision and UE-context release completed within 1.670s. TRACE-5G extends UE trust beyond admission without any modification of the standardized 5G protocols.

papers.title: AI-Induced Social Erosion: Using LLMs for Work Tasks Reduces Help-Seeking Intentions Towards Colleagues
papers.authors: Kevin Chow, Sophia Deng, Bowen He, Hanyi Min et al.
papers.summary: Generative AI is becoming embedded in knowledge work as an intelligent collaborator to assist in completing tasks. However, this readily available assistance risks displacing key interactions through which colleague relationships are built and sustained at work. This paper leverages the concept of help-seeking behaviour to investigate whether and how AI usage shapes colleague relationships. We conducted an online experimental vignette study where 248 knowledge workers evaluated scenarios that systematically varied whether and how AI was used across different work tasks. Using linear mixed-effects models, we found that AI-enabled work reduced help-seeking intentions compared to non-AI work across tasks, and especially for brainstorming. Visible AI usage was associated with greater help-seeking intentions towards colleagues, and individual contributors' colleague relationships were more vulnerable than managers. Our findings identify opportunities for workplace AI tools, practices, and policies to preserve colleague relationships in increasingly AI-integrated workplaces.

papers.title: AI Deactivation Reduces Loneliness and Increases Social Interaction
papers.authors: Dora Zhao, Grace Wang, Yutong Zhang, Lujain Ibrahim et al.
papers.summary: General-purpose artificial intelligence (AI) assistants are increasingly embedded in everyday life, transforming how people accomplish tasks and potentially reshaping how they interact with others. Prior research has focused on how using AI for explicitly social purposes affects users' psychological well-being and social lives. Yet such uses account for only a small portion of interactions with general-purpose AI assistants. Whether using AI for everyday, instrumental tasks affects users' psychological well-being and social behavior remains unclear. Here we investigate these effects through a longitudinal deactivation experiment with active ChatGPT users (N=625), in which participants were randomly assigned to abstain from using AI assistants for either fourteen days (treatment) or one day (control). Participants used AI predominantly for instrumental purposes, with 84.7% reporting productivity as their most frequent use case. Two weeks of deactivation significantly reduced loneliness relative to the control group (β= -0.10, p=0.03), with reductions persisting two weeks after participants resumed using AI (β= -0.16, p=0.02). Deactivation also significantly increased the number of people participants interacted with in person and the time they spent socializing over the intervention period. Open-ended responses indicate that during the deactivation period participants sought help from others for tasks they otherwise would have delegated to AI and redirected attention toward social interaction. Overall, our findings suggest that even when AI is used primarily to accomplish instrumental tasks, it may inadvertently reduce opportunities for social interaction and connection.

papers.title: Design and Evaluation of a Body-Machine Interface as an Alternative Control Paradigm for Pedal-based Sewing Machines
papers.authors: Ashrut Aryal, Rajiv Ranganathan, Ranjan Mukherjee
papers.summary: Body-machine interfaces (BoMIs) exploit body movements to control assistive devices; they have been evaluated primarily in tasks such as cursor control or robotic manipulation where the entire movement repertoire is devoted toward device control. However, tasks with multiple concurrent processes require the user to share the movement repertoire used for device control with other body movements for task execution. This issue is examined here in the context of sewing, where the sewing machine is typically controlled by a pedal in coordination with hand movements for guiding the fabric. We evaluated the learning of a trunk-controlled BoMI for sewing machine control, and compared it with conventional pedal control. Twenty-four novice participants (12 BoMI, 12 Pedal) completed 10 trials of a standardized sewing assessment followed by 3 trials of a transfer task. The BoMI mapped trunk movements to the sewing machine's full functional repertoire, which included continuous speed control of the needle, and discrete actions such as presser-foot and needle lifts. The two groups learned at comparable rates, showing similar completion times and error counts; for both groups, completion time reduced by approximately 30%. Additional analyses showed that the BoMI group had fewer presser-foot lift errors during training and fewer errors on the first transfer trial. Both groups also exhibited similar subjective workload. These findings collectively demonstrate that a BoMI interface can support sewing-machine control during concurrent manual activity, highlighting the potential for using BoMIs for increasing accessibility in industrial workplace contexts.

papers.title: Towards Restorative Urban Spaces: An Exploratory Field Study of Nature Videos on Public Multi-Display Signage
papers.authors: Yuri Mikawa, Takumi Yokosaka, Yuki Kubota, Kazushi Maruya
papers.summary: In recent years, multi-display signage (MDS) has become increasingly common in urban stations, plazas, and other public spaces, where it is primarily used to present advertisements and information. Beyond these conventional applications, MDS offers opportunities to shape people's experiences of public environments through spatially distributed and dynamic visual content. Motivated by the potential of mediated nature to support restorative experiences in urban environments, we conducted a nine-day exploratory field study in a free-admission area of a science museum, presenting artificial intelligence (AI)-generated nature videos across four displays and collecting 1,263 questionnaire responses. We combined three complementary analyses. First, structural equation modeling identified strong associations among perceived consistency across displays, presence, and self-reported restorative responses, consistent with our theoretically motivated model. Second, exploratory comparisons across video-presentation configurations revealed modest differences in consistency and restoration ratings, although these AI-generated videos did not significantly outperform the advertisement reference. Third, qualitative analysis of open-ended responses identified fascination, immersion, and restorative feelings, alongside concerns about naturalness, visual quality, and motion-related discomfort. Together, these findings provide empirical insights into MDS-mediated nature experiences, with implications for nature-video design and questionnaire refinement. They also inform a tentative conceptual extension of the model incorporating additional perceptual and evaluative factors.

papers.title: Plan your Self-Adaptation! Ontology-Mediated Task and Architecture Co-adaptation Planning for Robots
papers.authors: Gustavo Rezende Silva, Tobias John, Francisco Martín, Einar Broch Johnsen
papers.summary: Autonomous robots may need to adapt both their task plans and architectural configurations as operating conditions change. These decisions are interdependent: architectural configurations determine which actions a robot can perform, while task plans determine which capabilities are required. This paper presents PLANTA, an ontology-mediated approach to task and architecture co-adaptation that considers these dependencies during mission planning. PLANTA uses an ontology expressed in the Web Ontology Language to represent architectural alternatives and their associated functional and quality requirements, while the Planning Domain Definition Language defines task actions and mission goals. By automatically translating and integrating these models, PLANTA enables joint planning of task and reconfiguration actions. The approach uses satisficing planning and replans when changes during execution invalidate the current plan. PLANTA is evaluated in two robotic scenarios involving underwater inspection and ground navigation. The results support the feasibility of runtime co-adaptation and show lower planning time and memory consumption compared with optimal-policy generation in the evaluated navigation scenario, while producing plans of similar quality.

papers.title: WEVO: World Model-Enabled VLA Optimization for Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation
papers.authors: Qianzhong Chen, Muyuan Lin, Yuyin Sun, Mac Schwager et al.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve vision-language-action (VLA) policies beyond imitation, but humanoid exploration is unsafe and simulator RL can exploit residual sim-to-real gaps. We present WEVO, a teleoperation-free framework for post-training a whole-body humanoid VLA in an action-conditioned video world model (WM). Simulated manipulation and locomotion play data improve contact-dynamics and viewpoint-change prediction. A VLA trained on synthetic demonstrations collects 20 autonomous real robot rollouts per task to align the WM with deployment observations. The VLA, whole-body controller (WBC), and video WM then form a closed-loop RL environment with dense progress rewards. Across three real robot tasks, play data improves every evaluated WM metric and downstream policy success; video WM RL raises mean success from 23.3% to 75.0%, compared with 48.3% for real robot RL. We therefore leverage the complementary strengths of both environments: simulation provides policy initialization and broad coverage, while the video WM offers a deployment-aligned environment for policy improvement. Project website: https://qianzhong-chen.github.io/wevo.github.io/.

papers.title: A Synthetic Multi-Modal Testbed for Security Stress Testing of Agentic Counter-UAS Systems
papers.authors: Ivan A. Fernandez, Jingdao Chen
papers.summary: Agentic cyber-physical systems rely on perception and state estimation to support autonomous decisions. Degraded, inconsistent, or manipulated sensor observations can therefore propagate through an autonomous pipeline and create security-relevant failures. This work presents a synthetic Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) testbed developed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim for repeatable stress testing of perception and tracking algorithms supporting agentic decision-making. A simplified quadrotor follows scripted trajectories while co-located virtual sensors generate synchronized RGB, RTX LiDAR, and illustrative IR-like observations. The testbed varies target range, motion, clutter, occlusion, and sensor availability, with future stress cases including sensor dropout, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, and false observations. As an initial exemplar, a nonlinear coordinated-turn Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is evaluated over a 20-s maneuvering trajectory using LiDAR target-centroid measurements. Position error and uncertainty are compared as LiDAR observations degrade and are lost. The framework provides a reproducible environment for studying how sensing degradation affects downstream autonomous estimation and resilience in agentic C-UAS systems.

papers.title: Verify2Act: Critic-Guided Latent World Models for Verifying Language-Conditioned Manipulation Plans
papers.authors: Chrisantus Eze, Christopher Crick
papers.summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can propose multi-step manipulation plans, but they have no grounded model of how a scene will change, and the pixel-level world models that could check those plans are slow and drift over long horizons. We present Verify2Act, a modular verification framework that separates semantic action proposal from latent physical verification. A VLM proposes candidate plans, a latent world model (V2A-WM) imagines each of them in the DINOv2 feature space, and a dual-head critic checks the imagined rollouts for temporal consistency and goal satisfaction before anything is executed. V2A-WM extends recent flow-matching world models with cross-attention action grounding and a causal temporal history window. We deploy the full system on a low-cost robot arm, training the world model and critic only on data generated in a digital twin. Across six language-conditioned tasks, Verify2Act reaches 83.3% task success, compared with 61.7% for a latent world model without our architectural changes, 53.3% for the VLM alone, and 46.7% for a pixel-diffusion world model. It verified every plan it executed and incurred no planning-induced failures: all of its failed episodes were caused by low-level grasp or placement slips. In simulation, Verify2Act obtains the highest five-task chain success on CALVIN among the compared baselines with 30× fewer reflective VLM calls than pixel-diffusion verification, and the highest success on cluttered nut assembly.

papers.title: Ferrofluid Shape Control with Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Anthony Czubarow, Antonio Terpin, Raffaello D'Andrea
papers.summary: Ferrofluids are liquids containing magnetic nanoparticles, enabling shape control through external magnetic fields. This deformability supports their use as soft robotic bodies that can navigate confined spaces and manipulate objects. Their nonlinear continuum dynamics, however, make reliable control challenging. Existing work shows how spatial magnetic fields from electromagnet arrays can establish and maintain desired ferrofluid configurations. A complementary objective is to exploit the fluid's dynamics under limited actuation to reach prescribed shapes that may not be sustainable at equilibrium. Here, we use deep model-based reinforcement learning to control these transient shapes. Learning directly through physical interaction, our policies select current commands for a single fixed electromagnet based on visual observations, guiding the moving ferrofluid toward prescribed geometries. The learned policies repeatedly attain a variety of shapes spanning polygons, asterisks and pentominoes. These results demonstrate that learning directly from physical interaction enables reliable fluid shaping, opening new possibilities for controlling ferrofluid-based soft robots.

papers.title: Release-Bound Withdrawal Authorization for Bitcoin Custody
papers.authors: Jian Cui, Rui Zhu, Haixu Tang
papers.summary: A compromised cryptocurrency withdrawal backend can request signatures on unauthorized payments. Previously signed transactions may remain spendable after pause or become spendable again after a reorganization. Release-Bound Withdrawal Authorization (RBWA) orders permits against pause in a replicated journal and restores exposure when its closing evidence disappears from Bitcoin's active chain. An optional route delays large payouts and permits independent cold recovery. Direct payments confirm in one block on regtest, and staged payments confirm in three or seven at delays of two or six. After rollback, a replayed recovery can win or lose to an already exported mature payout. Authenticated receipts can revoke one signing lease in a shared wallet. In matched synthetic schedules, probes reduce permits through compromised leases from 20 to 9 out of 33, with one false fence. Two held-out HTTP workloads find equal fixed-threshold precision for boosted audit and probe-augmented detectors. The audit fields already expose the probe authentication outcome. Live tests verify an exact maintenance exception and add a file marker as a distinct source. The marker fences a compromised lease that RPC-only audit misses. Audit with the same file-read evidence also fences a reader who bypasses the probe. The results tie the benefit of active probing to which evidence the operator can obtain.

papers.title: Reject and Report: Forgery-Evident Undetectable Watermarks for Generative Image Models
papers.authors: Yihan Wang, Haochen Sun, Xi He, Yaoliang Yu et al.
papers.summary: Provenance schemes such as those based on content watermarks let images from a generative model be traced back to it. A practical watermarking scheme must be accurate at a low false-positive rate (FPR), robust under content-preserving processing, and undetectable. In addition, it must resist forgery; otherwise, even from a single watermarked image and a surrogate model, an adversary can imprint the watermark onto an arbitrary image or regenerate new content that carries it, falsely attributing harmful content to a model or making authentic photographs appear AI-generated. We argue that a watermarking scheme should not only reject forgeries but also report them: a forgery rejected as unwatermarked leaves no trace of the attempt. State-of-the-art forgery-resilient undetectable watermarking schemes, such as SemBind, fall short on both counts. External anomaly detectors that do report forgeries either miss most of them or falsely flag genuine images after common processing. We propose Tripwire-WM, the first forgery-evident framework for undetectable watermarks. It commits the semantics of the generated image to the magnitudes of the initial latent noise, which the sign-based watermarks leave unused, through a distribution-preserving embedding; a forged image carries a valid watermark but with a commitment that does not match its content, so the detector both rejects it and reports it as forged. Built on the pseudorandom code (PRC) watermark and Gaussian Shading++, Tripwire-WM provably preserves their undetectability. On MS-COCO, with the owner's own model as the surrogate, it accepts no imprinting forgery, compared with up to 55.0% for SemBind, and reports all of them as forged; it also accepts at most 1.8% of reprompting forgeries, against up to 46.2% for SemBind. Meanwhile, it accepts at least 99% of genuine watermarked images at 10⁻⁶ FPR and matches the robustness of the base schemes.

papers.title: Bridging vision-language reasoning and learned control for legged navigation in the wild
papers.authors: Takahiro Miki, Robin Schmid, Manthan Patel, Turcan Tuna et al.
papers.summary: Autonomous navigation in diverse real-world environments remains one of the greatest challenges in robotics. It demands both robust low-level motion control to handle diverse terrain and high-level reasoning to interpret environmental cues. We present ROAM (Robust Open-world Autonomous Mobility), a system that enables legged robots to perform kilometer-scale navigation in complex alpine and urban settings. ROAM combines the world knowledge of a Vision-Language Model (VLM), pre-trained on internet-scale data, with robust locomotion and local planning policies learned in simulation via reinforcement learning (RL). The VLM provides common-sense reasoning and semantic interpretation of the scene, assessing risks, interpreting signs, and producing semantic labels with associated navigation costs. An open-vocabulary segmentation module converts these labels into a dense, real-time risk map, which conditions two pre-trained RL policies responsible for agile locomotion and local navigation, effectively coupling high-level VLM reasoning with low-level physical control. Real-world experiments showed the system's ability to autonomously navigate a wide range of complex real-world environments. The robot completes kilometer-long hikes with minimal intervention, interprets signs to avoid danger, and evaluates its environment to identify safe areas on which to step. This work represents a step toward the reliable deployment of systems in unstructured environments. However, it also underscores the challenges that remain in VLM reliability and spatial reasoning, indicating that foundational models are a crucial component but not yet a complete solution for navigation in the wild.

papers.title: Benchmarking Open-Source O-RAN and 5G NTN Stacks on Embedded ARM Platforms for Space Payloads
papers.authors: Esteban Municio, Oscar Baselga, Oscar Lasierra, Gines Garcia-Aviles et al.
papers.summary: Regenerative satellite payloads, which host the 5G Next Generation Node B (gNB) onboard instead of transparently relaying the radio signal, are a key building block of the Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) integration that 3GPP started in Release 17. Combining them with the Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) architecture adds software-defined control through RAN Intelligent Controllers (RICs), enabling in-orbit reconfiguration, multi-tenancy, and data-driven radio resource management. Open-source implementations make this vision accessible to research institutions and New Space missions, yet there is little quantitative evidence on how they behave on the embedded processors that a satellite can actually carry. This paper presents an out-of-the-box experimental benchmark of two open-source gNB stacks (i.e., OpenAirInterface/Duranta and srsRAN/OCUDU), and two Near-Real-Time RICs (i.e., the ORAN-SC Near-RT RIC and FlexRIC). All components are deployed on an ARMv8 platform representative of the processing units used in small-satellite payloads, driving a USRP B210 software-defined radio. We compare them in terms of functional compliance (3GPP NTN features, O-RAN interfaces, multi-tenancy), resource efficiency, real-time behavior, and engineering suitability. Results show that these platforms can host a joint gNB + near-RT RIC deployment using any of the considered components, although further optimizations are still required for carrier-grade performance. However, the performance and standards compliance vary significantly among them. Building on these results, we derive a decision framework that maps mission profiles and Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) budgets to gNB/near-RT RIC combinations. Finally, we discuss the open gaps remaining before these stacks can be flown in NTN regenerative payloads.

papers.title: Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests
papers.authors: Rohith Pasula, Johari Dramiga, Viraj Shah, Suzan Halim et al.
papers.summary: Experimentation teams must decide which proposed website changes to test with live traffic. We evaluated whether forecasts from simulated shoppers could inform that choice. We screened 412 historical website A/B tests and evaluated four systems on the 318 that ran longer than 21 days. Each system predicted an original win, a variant win, or an inconclusive result. Page roles were masked and recorded outcomes were withheld during inference. Squoosh UX-1, a model fine-tuned on human browsing data, simulated 1,000 shoppers per arm and correctly classified 267 of 318 outcomes (84.0%, 95% Wilson interval 79.5-87.6%, treating experiments as independent). Qwen3 Next 80B, the strongest general-purpose configuration on outcome accuracy, correctly classified 196 of 318 (61.6%). UX-1 favored the variant in 126 experiments. In the live tests, 118 of those variants won (93.7%), four lost, and four had inconclusive results. The remaining 192 experiments included 19 additional variant wins.

papers.title: Ontology of Software Maintenance
papers.authors: Luis Olsina, Pablo Becker, Maria Fernanda Papa
papers.summary: Software maintenance is often a long and costly phase of the software lifecycle, encompassing activities such as defect correction, adaptation, code improvement, and functionality enhancement. Conceptual inconsistencies and terminological variation continue to hinder effective communication among researchers and practitioners. To address this gap, this paper presents the Software Maintenance Top-Domain Ontology (SwMaintTDO), a high-domain ontology developed within a five-tier ontological architecture. This ontology was constructed using competency questions, ontological analysis of documented maintenance processes, artifacts, and resources, and alignment with established software engineering standards. SwMaintTDO provides a unified and extensible conceptual model for representing key maintenance processes, roles, resources, artifacts, goal purposes, and the transition of target modifiable and context entities from current to updated maintenance situations. The applicability and value of SwMaintTDO are demonstrated through its application -via its concepts and relationships- to the process specification of a corrective maintenance strategy.

papers.title: User Perceptions of Deceptive In-Vehicle Infotainment User Interfaces
papers.authors: Pedram MohajerAnsari, Iwinosa Aideyan, Anna Galeano, Arjun Arunasalam et al.
papers.summary: Modern vehicles collect extensive data about drivers, passengers, and vehicle use, with privacy and consent decisions increasingly mediated through infotainment software. Although dark patterns have been widely studied in web, mobile, and e-commerce interfaces, little is known about how they appear in automotive infotainment systems or how users perceive them. We study this problem through Android Automotive OS (AAOS), conducting a three-phase empirical analysis. First, 26 HCI and privacy annotators audit four OEM AAOS emulators (Honda, Volvo, GM, and Polestar), documenting 17 dark-pattern types across 65 observations. Second, a user study with 100 participants compares OEM-specific implementations of five dark patterns across GMC, Honda, and Volvo, finding that implementation choices affect user perceptions. Third, an independent study with 49 participants compares automotive and e-commerce dark-pattern clips before and after a brief tutorial, showing that automotive's initial rating advantage largely collapses after instruction. Together, the studies identify a sophistication paradox: subtler dark patterns are less likely to trigger user suspicion and may therefore be harder to identify. These findings indicate that oversight should evaluate not just the presence but also the specific implementation of dark patterns.

papers.title: Formally Verified Semidefinite Programming
papers.authors: Perry Hart
papers.summary: We present a formally verified Rust implementation of a first-order semidefinite programming solver, a nontrivial piece of numerical software. We wrote the solver by hand and then directed Claude to generate the entire verification in Verus, an automated theorem prover for Rust programs. We discuss the algorithm underlying the solver, its implementation in Rust, and our pragmatic approach to proving it correct in Verus.

papers.title: Before the Choice: An Evidential Framework for Studying Prospective Representations in Language Models
papers.authors: Sion Israel Sion
papers.summary: An observable decision reveals the selected action but does not determine which alternatives were internally represented. Drawing on prospection research and hippocampal forward-sweep observations, we develop Before the Choice, an evidence-oriented framework distinguishing future-directed content, prospective computation, and causal guidance. The framework organizes four experimental contrasts and makes their alternative explanations explicit. Its first test case concerns unchosen trajectories in deterministic symbolic environments. A preregistered low-rank probe evaluated once on a sealed TEST did not meet its criterion (paired accuracy 0.020 versus 0.195 for a text-and-observed-choice baseline; 293 admissible pairs). Exploratory H1b exposed a reconstruction-by-elimination problem: identifying the chosen candidate can determine the unchosen target. In H1c, matched worlds varied an unchosen continuation while keeping candidate keys bitwise invariant. With specified positive controls passed, decoding in the late-key condition remained at 0.521 (p = 0.18; 141 contributing families). These observations do not identify prospective simulation or establish an absence of prospective representations. They illustrate why identifiability, sensitivity, and a dependence-aware null model must constrain inferences from decodability. PREM is proposed as an organizational framework and is not validated by these results. We offer it as a methodological contribution to empirical AI welfare research, which will require such evidential distinctions. Code and protocol records: https://github.com/besionisrael/before-choice

papers.title: Mutable State in Enrich-by-Need Security Protocol Analysis
papers.authors: Joshua D Guttman, Paul D Rowe, Eben Blaisdell
papers.summary: Security protocol analysis has emphasized message-passing, as this is how different principals interact in authentication, key exchange, and similar functionalities. However, in many protocols a principal also maintains mutable state that limits what actions its local sessions may take; this cross-session state is altered by other local sessions. In this paper we show how to represent this cross-session mutable state in the strand space approach to symbolic protocol analysis, and how to implement the resulting ideas in the Cryptographic Protocol Shapes Analyzer CPSA. The key theory is expressed in two axioms characterizing state, plus protocol-specific rules. It leads to tight, specific characterizations of protocol behavior in relevant cases, and aids in developing correct protocols relying on cross-session mutable state.

papers.title: TripleKV: Predict, Prefetch, Protect – KV Cache Management for AI Agents
papers.authors: Shashwat Jaiswal, Chloe Alverti, Mengmei Ye, Chen Wang et al.
papers.summary: LLM agents alternate between inference and tool execution, repeatedly reusing their growing context across calls. Under high concurrency, their combined key-value (KV) cache working set can reach hundreds of GiB, far exceeding GPU memory capacity. As idle KV cache blocks are evicted to slower storage tiers, returning agents incur expensive retrievals that stall inference. To address this problem, we present TripleKV, a three-tier KV cache management system that hides the delays of these retrievals. %exploits tool execution to hide these delays. In agentic workloads, the KV blocks needed by the next inference request are known in advance; only the time of their reuse is uncertain. TripleKV uses a tool-aware latency predictor to estimate when each tool call will complete and prefetches the required KV blocks from SSD into host DRAM ahead of time. Unlike GPU prefetching, this avoids reserving scarce GPU memory and interfering with concurrent inference requests. To further improve DRAM utilization, TripleKV eliminates duplication of GPU-resident blocks in DRAM, and introduces a victim-cache mechanism that refills blocks from SSD upon their eviction from GPU memory. Across data, web, and coding agents, TripleKV reduces the fraction of requests requiring critical-path SSD reads from 45–76% to under 10%. It also reduces P95 time to first token (TTFT) by up to 49% compared with vLLM extended with DRAM and SSD KV-cache tiers, and achieves 1.5-7× lower P95 TTFT than recent agent-aware systems.

papers.title: Berth: SLO-Preserving GPU Sharing Without New Preemption
papers.authors: Mohammadali Khodabandehlou, Mahdi Alizadeh, Lei Gao, Murali Annavaram et al.
papers.summary: Inference services keep GPUs reserved for their worst-case load, and most of that capacity sits idle. Filling it with best-effort work such as training is the obvious remedy, and latency is why it rarely happens: on a shared GPU, a request that must finish within milliseconds finds the best-effort job's kernels running or queued ahead of it. Spatial sharing cannot evict them, temporal sharing gives the request only its turn, and hardware partitioning protects it by idling what it does not use. Systems that keep both the SLO and the utilization have reached inside the stack (rewriting kernels, patching the driver, instrumenting the framework), which the operator of a closed GPU stack cannot do. This paper argues that reaching inside is unnecessary. The time-slicer built into commodity GPUs already preempts a running kernel within a fraction of a millisecond and switches the moment a context runs out of work; what it lacks is priority, and priority can be created from outside by controlling what the best-effort context has to run. Berth is a user-space system built on this observation: a preloaded shim feeds the best-effort job to the GPU only when no request needs it (feed control), a declared deadline reference extends the rule to continuous-batching LLM engines, and a shortened best-effort time slice, set without privileges, bounds what a long kernel can cost. Berth changes no application, framework, kernel or driver. Across 31 scenario points with MLPerf SLOs and 13 baselines, Berth meets SLOs within a few percentage points of running alone, above every baseline, with 2.7-3.5x the best-effort throughput of the strongest ones; beside LLM serving, it meets per-token targets for nearly every request while training keeps running. Sharing a closed GPU under SLOs needs no new preemption mechanism, only control over what the existing one sees.

papers.title: Living off the Local Model: Abusing Browser-Embedded Language Models for Post-Exploitation
papers.authors: William Fleshman, Joseph Lucas
papers.summary: Browsers now ship local language models to ordinary endpoints. Google includes Gemini Nano in Chrome to enable productivity features such as summarization, with inference running entirely on the device. These browser-embedded models provide new living-off-the-land opportunities for attackers, each instance a potential post-exploitation engine already installed, signed by the vendor, and invisible to network monitoring. The Gemini model is multimodal, capable of processing files, analyzing screenshots, or conversing with an attacker. We show that it can be driven from the host using only interpreters that ship with the operating system and find that the one-time user-activation check before the model is downloaded is easily satisfied with a simulated click or bypassed entirely. We measure and report the current model's ability to identify credentials on the host, detect PII in email, classify images, and call custom tools. We combine these capabilities and use the model to carry out a simulated cyber operation: reading a password from a webcam image, unlocking an encrypted archive, triaging the contents, and staging a private key for exfiltration, end-to-end without user-interaction.

papers.title: Twindex: Index Cache Offloading with Coarse-to-Fine Selection for Long-Context Sparse-Attention Serving
papers.authors: Yuxuan Xia, Jiakun Fan, Han Meng, Hao Mark Chen et al.
papers.summary: In long-context decoding, GPU memory (HBM) caps how many requests a GPU decodes at once. Sparse-attention models such as Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek V4.1-Flash and GLM-5.2 add an indexer: at every step it scores all past index entries with its own indexer cache, and attention reads the main KV of only the top-k entries. We find that once serving systems move the main KV to host memory, the indexer cache becomes the HBM bottleneck, at 63% of per-request HBM on Qwen and 75% on V4.1 at 1M tokens. Therefore, we introduce Twindex, which keeps only a compact copy of the indexer cache in HBM and the full indexer cache in host memory. At each step, the copy selects a larger candidate set, and the model's own indexer picks the top-k from the original rows of the candidates in host memory. The copy combines the shared component with the compressed residuals, both learned once offline. Twindex changes no model weights and runs inside CUDA graphs. At 1M tokens on modern GPUs, Twindex fits 1.78×, 1.62× and 3.03× as many requests as KV offloading alone on Qwen, V4.1 and GLM-5.2, and reaches 1.44×, 1.25× and 2.54× decode throughput when host memory does not limit the batch. Every request keeps its own index, and Qwen and GLM requests share prefix main KV in host memory. In our evaluations, mean benchmark scores are at most 3.1% below the baseline's.

papers.title: DVBench: End-to-End Benchmark for Real-World UVM Design Verification Agents
papers.authors: Jiaru Qian, Jiawei Li, Xiaolong Hu, Zheng Shen et al.
papers.summary: Design verification (DV) remains a major bottleneck in hardware development, with large-scale verification using the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) being highly labor-intensive. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer new opportunities for DV automation. However, existing benchmarks primarily construct mutually decoupled subtasks, which deviates from the real-world workflow. In this paper, we present DVBench, the first end-to-end benchmark for Real-World UVM design verification agents. DVBench comprises 95 tasks across 9 functional domains and 5 difficulty levels, covering diverse verification scenarios and design scales. Each task requires agents to independently complete the full verification workflow. DVBench evaluates final testbenches via compilation, coverage, and bug detection, while assessing intermediate artifacts including feature lists, test plans, and reference models. We evaluate frontier LLMs (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra) and agent frameworks (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode). Experimental results show that the best LLM-based agent (Codex & GPT-6 Astra) can only achieve an overall success rate of 21.05%, revealing substantial room for improvement in complex verification tasks.

papers.title: Agentic Harness Engineering Beta: Requirement-Centered Evolution of Agent Harnesses
papers.authors: Jiahang Lin, Jiahao Chen, Yiding Wang, Shichun Liu et al.
papers.summary: Real-world harness engineering is driven by explicit and implicit user requirements, which guide development and validation. However, existing harness evolution methods often overlook implicit requirements and interaction needs, while using a single evolution agent to modify the harness and benchmark scores to select changes. This process often produces narrow patches and leads to benchmark-specific local optima. We introduce Agentic Harness Engineering Beta (AHE-Beta), a requirement-centered loop that brings real-world engineering practices into harness evolution. The loop consists of three steps: (1) User-driven evaluation lets simulated users raise their requirements as issues while they work with the harness over multiple turns. (2) Team-based modification implements those requirements as generalizable changes rather than task-specific patches. (3) Requirement-driven selection merges a change only when it resolves a verified requirement and passes review. Empirically, on held-out tasks, AHE-Beta raises pass@1 from 21.9% to 33.3% while using 40.8% fewer tokens than Base Harness, and achieves higher pass@1 than Claude Code, Meta-Harness, and AHE. In a blind human A/B test, real users prefer AHE-Beta in 31 of 48 valid pairs and rate it higher on all five dimensions, matching the directional preference of the user simulator. The human A/B results show that AHE-Beta achieves its goal of aligning harness evolution with real-world user requirements. Without further evolution, the gains transfer to GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash with pass@1 improvements of 15.8% and 5.3% over Base Harness. Together, these results show that requirement-centered harness evolution is a more general method for improving agent capabilities.

papers.title: Mine Locally, Verify Globally: Exact Recovery, Compilation, and Distortion of Mined Temporal Rules
papers.authors: Nikolaos Kekatos, Priyanka Sinha, Stylianos Basagiannis, Antonio Anastasio Bruto da Costa et al.
papers.summary: Specification mining extracts temporal rules that describe relationships between events in recorded system traces. Applying these rules in distributed monitoring systems is more difficult because observations come from different nodes, whose clocks may not be synchronized, and events may be lost or reordered during transmission. In this paper, we study how to aggregate the coverage of mined rules across observers, determine whether their temporal windows are needed during monitoring, and characterize their detection under event loss. Our evaluation uses IPv6 packet traces collected from 21 receivers across four continents. We show that local mining followed by global confirmation recovers centralized rule coverage under suitable conditions while substantially reducing communication overhead. In contrast, merging traces with unaligned clocks can distort coverage by introducing incorrect temporal matches. A window-gain criterion identifies rules that require temporal state, while our loss analysis and broker experiments demonstrate why contiguous losses can be more damaging than independent losses. The results identify separate requirements for aggregating observations, selecting monitor state, and handling event loss.

papers.title: WorldRuler: Interactive World Modeling under Configurable Rules
papers.authors: Mingliang Zhai, Chuanhao Li, Jiaming Tan, Zhen Li et al.
papers.summary: Rules govern how player actions change interactive worlds. Different rules create distinct gameplay experiences within similar scenes and action spaces. For customizable gameplay, generative world models must follow user-defined rules beyond real-world behaviors. However, realizing user-defined rules presents two challenges: Rule-State Persistence and Rule-to-Visual Realization. The former requires preserving rule definitions, dependencies, and world states across saving and loading, so that restored worlds follow the established rules. The latter requires accurately realizing rule-induced changes on designated objects and attributes, particularly when affected objects are unseen. In this paper, we propose WorldRuler, which organizes rule definitions, dependencies, and object states in an executable 3D rule graph and connects rule execution, video generation, and perceptual feedback in a closed loop. The graph supports joint saving and restoration of rules and world states, while dynamic object binding grounds rule-specified entities in visual instances and uses stored states to constrain generation from their first appearance. We further introduce object attribute state replacement and counterfactual reconstruction training, enabling accurate attribute control and compatible appearance and motion changes while limiting interference with unrelated content. We develop an automated data collection and annotation pipeline using GTA-V and Habitat to construct RuleVerse, a dataset of rule-driven interactions with detailed state and event annotations, including cases where rules take effect before affected objects become visible. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of WorldRuler in preserving rule-state consistency across saving and loading and accurately realizing rule outcomes on designated objects and attributes.

papers.title: MLIR-MRacle: Memory-Model-Aware Metamorphic Fuzzing of Concurrent MLIR
papers.authors: Aaron Gabayoyo, Aidan Dakhama, Ajitha Rajan
papers.summary: Multi-level compilers built on MLIR lower concurrent programs through many stages towards targets with potentially drastically different memory models, where an optimisation which appears reasonable, can silently change program behaviour. Testing these lowerings is hard: a concurrent program often has no single expected outcome, and existing MLIR fuzzers often assume determinism. We present MLIR-MRacle, a memory-model-aware metamorphic fuzzer for concurrent MLIR programs. MLIR-MRacle applies metamorphic relations gated by the target memory model, so that both the original and transformed programs remain well defined - executing both repeatedly, and comparing their outcome sets or distributions withone of two statistical oracles. A coverage guided campaign driver built on libafl is used to perform continuous fuzzing. MRs, memory models, oracles, and execution backends all provide extension points for future researchers and compiler engineers to build off this package. In a case study on Armv8 hardware, MLIR-MRacle ran over 145k trials across four configurations, reaching up to 93.6k compiler coverage edges, and found a bug in the OpenMP dialect verifier that has since been fixed upstream. Video: https://youtu.be/lKtGk0H97Ts?si=dWLUHl2CJ24ep6JY

papers.title: Exploring Speaker-Aware Engagement Modeling for Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder
papers.authors: Kaleen Shrestha, Austin Joel Dympep, Young Suh Hong, Maja Matarić
papers.summary: Prior work on engagement modeling in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) has demonstrated substantial individual variability in behavioral features, particularly in visual modalities. In this work, we extend the literature to acoustic features in naturalistic interactions, where multiple speakers and atypical interaction patterns complicate speaker-specific analysis. We investigated whether speaker diarization improved acoustic engagement modeling during month-long, in-home socially assistive robot (SAR) interventions with seven children with ASD. We trained classical machine learning models using acoustic features extracted from diarized child and parent/caregiver audio and compared their performance with models trained on undiarized audio. Diarized audio consistently yielded higher area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values, although these differences were not statistically significant. More importantly, the relative contributions of child and caregiver acoustic features varied across participants, indicating that the acoustic information associated with engagement was not consistent across children. These findings extend evidence of participant-level variability in ASD engagement modeling to the acoustic domain and demonstrate the feasibility of isolating speaker-specific vocalizations for studying engagement in complex, naturalistic interactions.

papers.title: Sex Differences in the Detection of Parkinson's Disease from Speech
papers.authors: Hiba Akhaddar, Peter Plantinga, Mirco Ravanelli, Tristan Glatard
papers.summary: Parkinson's disease (PD) is the second most common neurodegenerative disease in the world, and 70% to 75% of PD patients suffer from speech disorders at some stage. Since PD affects men more frequently than women, previous publications tend to rely on unbalanced datasets that potentially introduce sex biases into trained models. This study investigates sex differences in PD detection from speech using deep learning and traditional machine learning approaches. We evaluated speech-based PD detection using embeddings from three pre-trained speech models, combined with handcrafted acoustic features and different classifiers. Sex-specific experiments were conducted on balanced subsets of four sustained phonation datasets, controlling for sex, disease status, and, where possible, age. All recordings were obtained during a sustained phonation task. Results show that female speakers were more accurately classified than male speakers in the larger dataset. Sex-specific results show that when the models are trained on one sex, they fail to generalize to the other one. Our results highlight the importance of including sex as a variable in the development of PD detection systems.

papers.title: Can Bandits Learn to Share a Channel? Distributed Multi-Armed Bandits for Slotted ALOHA
papers.authors: Kamil Szczech, Maksymilian Wojnar, Krzysztof Rusek, Katarzyna Kosek-Szott et al.
papers.summary: Slotted ALOHA networks constitute a playground for research on machine learning (ML)-based channel access schemes. We consider ML agents deployed in such networks and operating under severe constraints: fully distributed (independent operation), fully online (no pre-training), aperiodic (no fixed schedule), and with no explicit coordination (no signaling). We ask whether a multi-armed bandit (MAB), a minimal reinforcement learning agent, can learn the optimal policy for a capture-free slotted ALOHA system. We evaluate several MAB algorithms on aggregate network throughput and per-node fairness. Our best-performing agent is based on a Softmax bandit, which we call SALSA (Softmax ALOHA Learning for Shared Access). SALSA learns a per-node transmission policy close to optimal, with throughput near the theoretical maximum for fair random access. We achieve performance comparable to a competing state-of-the-art solution, but without requiring a priori knowledge of the network size.

papers.title: Movie2Game-Bench: Holistic Evaluation of Film-to-Game Adaptation Beyond Playability
papers.authors: Jialing Xie, Yifan Zhou, Yiwen Zhang, Junjun He
papers.summary: Adapting a film into a game requires selecting source elements and translating them into player actions, rules, and feedback. We introduce Movie2Game-Bench (M2G-bench), a benchmark for evaluating film-to-game adaptation beyond playability. M2G-bench combines general evaluation, movie-specific evaluation, and playtesting by three GUI model players. The protocol connects source content to gameplay steps and implementation evidence, capturing both content preservation and interactive realization. The benchmark comprises 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items. Evaluating 14 models on the same films with their selected primary harnesses reveals complementary strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. A shared weakness concerns playable sequences: this category has the lowest content-presence mean in all 14 models, averaging 37.9 out of 100 compared with 54.8 for iconic elements. Among judgments of retained emotionaldevelopment content, narrative choices account for 60.0% and scenario operation for 7.2%. These findings identify two linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation: preserving source situations that can support gameplay and connecting retained content to player actions and consequences.

papers.title: UEmo-D1: An Efficient and Calibrated Decision Model for Unified Multimodal Emotion Recognition
papers.authors: Daiqing Wu, Junqiao Wang, Chengyang Fang, Runhao Zeng et al.
papers.summary: Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) seeks to identify emotions conveyed through or elicited by media comprising diverse modality compositions. Research in this field has largely evolved along two paradigms: task-specific models and approaches based on Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). Despite their distinct strengths, neither fully reconciles three capabilities essential to human-like emotion understanding: cross-task generalization, efficient decision-making, and receptiveness to multiple plausible interpretations. Inspired by recent advances in decision models, we explore a unified framework that maps multimodal inputs, guided by natural language instructions, directly to distributions over candidate options, addressing these requirements through direct probabilistic decisions. We instantiate this framework in UEmo-D1, the first decision model for MER to our knowledge. To support joint training and systematic evaluation, we also curate UEmo-Data, comprising 977,270 training samples and 41 evaluation subsets across six MER tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate UEmo-D1's combination of strong recognition performance, low inference latency, and well-calibrated confidence estimates. Complementary analyses further reveal how training strategies and data composition influence these capabilities, providing practical insights into unified MER modeling. Together, our findings establish decision models as a feasible direction toward human-level emotion recognition. Project page: https://github.com/wdqqdw/UEmo-D1.

papers.title: Harmonic Circuit: Chord Progression Lies in a Sparse Principal Information Flow in Symbolic Music Models
papers.authors: Ruiji Yu, Gus Xia
papers.summary: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) seeks to decode neural network computations into human-understandable logic. A core methodology in MI is circuit discovery: identifying the information flow in sub-networks that drive specific model behaviors. While circuit discovery has matured within Natural Language Processing (NLP), the interpretable circuits in music models remain largely unexplored. In this work, we identify a music-functional circuit within two symbolic music generative models: ChatMusician and MuPT. The music function we consider is the prediction of the terminal tonic root in a classical harmonic progression pattern I … V → I. We use the Auto-Emergence algorithm to extract a principal sparse sub-network as the identified circuit. Validation via causal intervention confirms that this identified circuit is a primary driver of harmonic progression behaviors in the symbolic music models. To our knowledge, this represents the first systematic circuit-discovery study conducted within the music domain. Our demo page is available at: https://ukiyo23rui.github.io/auto-emergence-demo/.

papers.title: The landscape of AI speech generation and deepfake detection
papers.authors: Simon King
papers.summary: Synthetic speech has reached a level of naturalness that can deceive listeners into believing they are hearing natural speech. This opens up the possibility of using synthetic speech deepfakes to mislead both human listeners and automated systems. One response to this threat is to attempt to automatically detect deepfakes. This report offers the reader a self-contained overview of the landscape of synthetic speech generation and speech deepfake detection. It is intended to be accessible to a general audience and therefore includes brief histories of both fields, definitions of all acronyms, a glossary of technical terms, and an extensive bibliography for those who wish to read more.

papers.title: Probing Physics in Motion Diffusion Models Against Their Own Estimate
papers.authors: Saeed Ghorbani
papers.summary: Recent studies report that video diffusion models "know more than they show": physical properties decode better from their activations than from their inputs or outputs. But a diffusion model computes its clean-sample estimate from those same activations, so such a comparison measures how easily a readout extracts the information. Whether the model hides anything is a separate question. We set out to find hidden physical knowledge in kinematic text-to-motion diffusion models, where the physics of every intermediate estimate can be computed exactly, and recorded every layer along the sampling trajectories of MDM (two checkpoints) and MotionDiffuse. Against the usual baselines the layers do look ahead of the model's own estimate on balance and flight. With every readout tuned the same way, the estimate closes the gap: for balance and flight, adding a layer gains at most 0.01, a size that a positive control shows we would detect. The fall rate of jumps is the one clear exception. Early in denoising, MDM's layers add about 0.08 in R² (up to 0.11 in a refit) that the estimate does not yet show, and the gain fades as sampling proceeds; on MotionDiffuse it is small and not robust. The estimate also flags floating samples without training, but aborting them saves under a tenth of the compute. In a video model, plausibility that linear probes miss in Wan 2.1's clean latent becomes readable after one fixed nonlinearity.

papers.title: MINT: Meeting-time Indicators for Truncation in Multi-Step Off-Policy RL
papers.authors: Seungyub Han, Taehyun Cho, Dohyeong Kim, Kyungjae Lee et al.
papers.summary: Many multi-step off-policy temporal-difference methods handle policy mismatch through products of per-step trace coefficients, leading to a trade-off between variance control and long-horizon signal. The maximum trace length consequently becomes a sensitive hyperparameter. We propose MINT (Meeting-time INdicators for Truncation), which replaces these products with a binary stopping indicator: one until coupled behavior and target trajectories first meet, zero thereafter. At the true value function, the indicator's idempotence yields a variance bound governed by meeting-time survival. For practical implementation, a single sampled action provides a model-free surrogate for the stopping rule, requiring no transition model or mixing-time estimate. We derive separate sufficient conditions for contraction of the state-coupled operator and its practical surrogate under fixed-policy evaluation. On MuJoCo and DeepMind Control tasks, MINT outperforms the reported multi-step baselines; the main MuJoCo comparison uses a common cap without per-task cap-length tuning. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of MINT on Atari 100k, RWRL, and OGBench experiments; MINT adapts the backup horizon to reduce target variability relative to long fixed-horizon backups across tasks and dynamics.

papers.title: RespCCT and FreqCCT: Compact, Explainable and Cost-Aware Convolutional Transformers for Multi-Class Respiratory Disease Classification
papers.authors: Auntor Chakma, Mst. Farhana Akter, Abu Henaf Rashid Ahmad Mufti, Asmana Yasmin
papers.summary: Chest auscultation depends on the listener, and software that classifies lung sounds could give a second reading where trained listeners are scarce. The most accurate published classifiers fine-tune large pretrained networks, and their accuracy is rarely reported with running cost or paired statistics. This study makes three contributions. (i) It proposes RespCCT and FreqCCT, two compact convolutional transformers of 173,187 and 124,999 parameters that learn from random initialization on mel, constant-Q and cepstral images of 5 s frames from three public databases, ICBHI, KAUH and RD@TR, with 1,665 audio files in seven classes. (ii) It compares both models with five ImageNet-pretrained networks and larger distilled variants on one test set, using paired bootstrap intervals. (iii) It measures the cost of every pipeline stage on one CPU thread, tests whether attribution maps depend on the trained weights, and probes whether the learned features reveal the recording source. On the test fold, RespCCT reaches an accuracy of 98.13% and a macro F1 of 0.970, and FreqCCT reaches 97.58% and 0.951. Over five folds, RespCCT with three seeds reaches 97.65% and 0.959, and FreqCCT with one seed reaches 96.95% and 0.941. The two strongest pretrained networks reach a macro F1 of 0.984, whereas RespCCT needs 2.0 to 64.6 times less weight storage. Computing the three input images takes longer than running either model, and a linear probe identifies the source database with 0.958 accuracy. A team can weigh accuracy against storage and time before device testing.

papers.title: OpenKAGE: Open-Ended Lifelong Learning in the Open World via Knowledge-Sharing Agent-Group Evolution
papers.authors: Wenhao Yuan, Longhui Yuan, Zexi Jia, Ningzhe Shi et al.
papers.summary: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

papers.title: Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through Environment-Player Co-Development
papers.authors: Xirui Jiang, Yuxi Chen, Rui Yang, Feng Luo et al.
papers.summary: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game environments and players to collect diverse and verifiable gameplay experience at scale. In the Game2Player loop, a Builder agent adapts existing web games, exposes their internal state, and defines tasks with state-based progress measures and success checks. A Coding Player and a VLM Player then attempt the tasks and report problems to the Builder for repair, so that play serves as both environment validation and training data collection. With Game2Player, we build 568 verified web games with 3,436 tasks, collect 15.7K trajectories (307 hours of gameplay), and hold out 50 games as the benchmark PlayerBench. To evaluate the collected experience as training data, we train VLM agents with progress-weighted SFT, assigning greater weight to steps that advance task progress. Game2Player-9B improves progress from 14.3% to 31.2% on PlayerBench and from 30.0% to 53.1% on the external GameWorld benchmark. More broadly, our work suggests a path for visual agents to scale their gameplay experience by building, verifying, and learning from existing game worlds.

papers.title: Option-GRPO: Hierarchical RL Against AI Slop in Code Generation for Unseen SDKs
papers.authors: Prashank Kadam
papers.summary: Large language models increasingly produce AI slop in generated code: verbose, redundant, non-idiomatic implementations that pass functional checks but bloat codebases. The problem compounds on SDKs released after the model's training cutoff, where the model has neither idiomatic priors nor compositional understanding. We present Option-GRPO, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that adapts a code LLM to an unseen SDK from its source code alone, without human-written usage examples or test cases, and that explicitly optimizes for both functional correctness and code elegance. Our key insight is that SDK source code contains compositional structure that defines a hierarchy of reusable code patterns (code options) which simultaneously serve as the building blocks of a curriculum and the action space for efficient policy optimization. We show that code options induce a valid semi-Markov decision process, give conditional bounds under which shorter option description length implies more concise and, in expectation, more API-efficient programs, and analyze under stated assumptions how the option hierarchy improves credit assignment by a factor of T/K. Using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with execution-based rewards at each curriculum level, Option-GRPO discovers SDK idioms, composes them into patterns, and assembles patterns into complete programs. Experiments on 12 unseen SDKs with a 32B-parameter base model demonstrate 61.4% pass@1, outperforming flat GRPO by 8.7 points, ExploraCoder by 11.2 points, and ReCode by 6.3 points. Option-GRPO produces solutions that use 34.7% fewer API calls and are 27% shorter than flat-GRPO outputs while maintaining higher correctness, directly attacking the slop problem.

papers.title: FairPGT: Partitioned Graph Transformers for Dual-Level Fair Graph Clustering
papers.authors: Siamak Ghodsi, Amjad Seyedi, Sahar Tahmasebi, Eirini Ntoutsi et al.
papers.summary: Clustering on attributed graphs can produce demographically biased clusters, particularly when communities align with protected groups. Graph transformers can amplify this bias through same-group attention, while global attention limits scalability. We propose FairPGT, a partitioned graph transformer for fair graph clustering. FairPGT restricts attention to METIS partitions and connects them through routing tokens, which divides the quadratic cost of attention by the number of partitions. A graph-aware self-training target guides clustering, with a provably bounded deviation from the standard DEC target. Fairness is imposed at two levels: a mutual-information term promotes demographic parity in cluster assignments, while a normalized cross-group attention ratio (nCGAR) guides attention toward group neutrality through self-distillation. We prove that the nCGAR correction moves attention toward neutrality and establish a condition preventing overshooting. Across seven benchmarks, FairPGT achieves the best clustering performance and statistical parity on the three largest graphs (Credit, Pokec-n, Pokec-z), with a statistical-parity gap approximately ten times lower than DMoN, and is Pareto-dominated on only one dataset. On controlled stochastic block models, FairPGT attains 97% of the derived upper bound on NMI for exactly fair clustering when communities and protected groups coincide. These graphs further show that, under strong alignment, assignment-level fairness alone makes the attention group-heterophilous, whereas attention-level fairness alone improves neutrality without ensuring fair clusters. Code for reproducibility is available at https://github.com/SiamakGhodsi/FairPGT.

papers.title: What Interpolators Store and What They Express: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Benign Overfitting and Label-Free Model Selection
papers.authors: Nikolaos Nikolaou
papers.summary: Overparameterized learners can fit noisy training labels perfectly and still predict well, which neither classical complexity measures nor information-theoretic generalization bounds explain. We develop an information-theoretic framework that separates two things an interpolating learner does with its sample: storage, the information the trained model retains about its training labels, and expression, the information about the sample that reaches its predictions at fresh inputs. We first characterize the ideal model: for a loss l, the least complex l-sufficient representation is the Bayes act, whose entropy is the minimal sufficient complexity; this generalizes, and corrects, an earlier "lossless maximal compression" view of boosting. We then show that every interpolator stores exactly nH(Y|X) bits of label noise, so storage, and bounds built on it (including CMI bounds), cannot tell interpolators apart. Expression can: excess risk is bounded above and below by the expressed information V, the entropy over training samples of the prediction at an input, plus a modal-bias term, exactly so for binary labels. Benign overfitting is therefore vanishing expression, a picture that covers nearest-neighbour rules, averaging, minimum-norm least squares and double descent, and that links V to classical bias-variance decompositions and to model disagreement. Finally, V gives a model-selection criterion that needs no held-out labels. Among overparameterized learners on 15 noisy datasets, V estimated from two disjoint halves has 60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost and matches 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of its cost; at matched cost it also beats selection by conditional mutual information. We characterize when it fails and give remedies. Code: https://github.com/nnikolaou/GLMC

papers.title: LoRN: Low-Rank Noise Steering for Generative Robot Policies
papers.authors: Wei Liu, Abrar Anwar, Huihua Zhao, Soha Pouya et al.
papers.summary: Noise steering improves pretrained generative robot policies by learning to select their initial noise without updating model weights. We find that actions in the evaluated world-action models are more sensitive to video noise than action noise, making video noise an expressive input for steering. However, the noise-steering methods we evaluate, in their published forms, struggle to scale to the high-dimensional noise inputs of large policy classes such as world-action models. We introduce Low-Rank Noise Steering (LoRN), a reinforcement learning method that scales noise steering to world-action models.
